title: Cardiovascular System
tagline: The heart and circulation, the ECG, hypertension, coronary disease, heart failure and arrhythmias
summary: Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death worldwide. This course explains how the heart and circulation work and how they are controlled, how to read the ECG, and the causes, recognition and principles of management of hypertension, coronary artery disease, heart failure, arrhythmias, valve and congenital heart disease, and diseases of the arteries and veins.
overview: The cardiovascular system has two parts: a pump, the heart, with its chambers, valves and electrical system; and a network of vessels whose pressures and resistances decide where the blood goes. Clinical cardiology follows the same division. Some patients have a failing or misfiring pump; others have a blocked, leaking, torn or clotted vessel. This course keeps both in view and teaches the physiology that explains them.

It starts with the cardiac cycle, cardiac output and the pressure–volume loop, then the cardiac action potentials and the 12-lead ECG. Next come blood flow, blood pressure and its regulation over seconds, hours and days. The clinical chapters follow: hypertension, the largest modifiable cause of cardiovascular disease; atherosclerosis, angina and the acute coronary syndromes; heart failure and the neurohormonal model that explains why four drug classes prolong life; the arrhythmias and atrial fibrillation; valve disease, endocarditis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and congenital heart disease; and finally aneurysm, dissection, peripheral arterial disease and venous thromboembolism.

Each chapter moves from mechanism to bedside: why the heart sounds and the jugular venous pulse look and sound as they do, why aortic stenosis causes syncope on exertion, how a troponin result should be read, and how much a treatment reduces absolute risk. Worked cases and calculations (cardiac output by Fick, QTc, valve area, ABPI, numbers needed to treat) appear throughout. UK guidance from NICE is followed, with European and American guidance noted where they differ; the course explains the principles of management and is not a substitute for current local guidelines.
outcomes: Describe the phases of the cardiac cycle and explain the heart sounds, the jugular venous pulse and the arterial pulse in terms of valve and chamber events.
Explain the determinants of cardiac output, the Frank–Starling principle, the Fick principle and the pressure–volume loop.
Explain cardiac action potentials and the conduction system, and interpret a 12-lead ECG systematically, including rate, axis, intervals, QTc, bundle branch block, ischaemia and electrolyte changes.
Apply the relationships between pressure, flow and resistance to blood pressure, oedema and shock, and describe the short- and long-term regulation of blood pressure.
Classify and confirm hypertension using NICE NG136, assess target-organ damage and secondary causes, and outline the principles of drug treatment.
Explain the pathogenesis of atherosclerosis, investigate stable chest pain, interpret troponin, and outline reperfusion and secondary prevention in the acute coronary syndromes.
Define and classify heart failure, explain its neurohormonal basis, interpret natriuretic peptides, and outline the medicines and devices that change its course.
Recognise the common bradycardias and tachycardias, explain the mechanisms of arrhythmia, and apply stroke-risk scoring and anticoagulation principles in atrial fibrillation.
Correlate valve lesions with their haemodynamics and murmurs, recognise infective endocarditis and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and explain the physiology of common congenital heart lesions.
Recognise peripheral arterial disease, acute limb ischaemia, aortic aneurysm and dissection, and venous thromboembolism, and outline the principles of their investigation and management.

history.title: The circulation of the blood
history.detail: William Harvey's De Motu Cordis argues from the valves of the heart and veins, and from the volume pumped with each beat, that the blood moves in a circle, driven by the heart.

history.title: Measuring blood pressure
history.detail: Stephen Hales connects a glass tube to the artery of a horse and sees the blood rise about eight feet and rise and fall with each beat, the first measurement of arterial pressure.

history.title: The foxglove
history.detail: William Withering publishes An Account of the Foxglove, describing how digitalis relieves the oedema of 'dropsy', much of which was heart failure.

history.title: The cuff
history.detail: Scipione Riva-Rocci introduces the inflatable arm cuff; in 1905 Nikolai Korotkoff describes the sounds heard below it, making blood pressure measurement routine.

history.title: The electrocardiogram
history.detail: Willem Einthoven records clear human electrocardiograms with his string galvanometer, names the P, Q, R, S and T waves and defines the limb leads; he receives the Nobel Prize in 1924.

history.title: A catheter in the heart
history.detail: Werner Forssmann passes a urinary catheter from a vein in his own arm into his right atrium and confirms its position by X-ray; cardiac catheterisation later becomes a standard method of measuring pressures and output.

history.title: Surgery for blue babies
history.detail: Alfred Blalock, following Helen Taussig's reasoning and with a technique worked out by Vivien Thomas, creates a subclavian-to-pulmonary artery shunt for a child with tetralogy of Fallot.

history.title: The heart–lung machine
history.detail: John Gibbon uses a heart–lung machine to close an atrial septal defect, showing that the circulation can be maintained outside the body while the heart is opened.

history.title: Coronary angioplasty
history.detail: Andreas Gruentzig performs the first percutaneous coronary angioplasty in Zurich, the start of catheter-based treatment of coronary disease.

references.title: Levick's Introduction to Cardiovascular Physiology (6th edition)
references.note: A clear account of cardiovascular physiology, from the cardiac cycle to the control of the circulation.

references.title: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology (14th edition)
references.note: Standard physiology textbook; its chapters on cardiac output, venous return and the renal control of blood pressure underlie several chapters here.

references.title: The ECG Made Easy (10th edition)
references.note: A short, practical introduction to reading the electrocardiogram.
